evidence_quote: DSC was acquired by Unilever for a reported $1 billion in cash.
prompt: Two founders want to sell razor blades by mail on a monthly subscription, at a very low price, against two dominant brands that spend heavily on advertising. They do not make the blades themselves and would resell a supplier's products. Proposal (2012): launch with a low-budget humorous online video and take orders at once on a simple website. Risks raised: the dominant brands could cut prices or sue; the company depends on one outside supplier; a single video may bring little traffic; customers may not like buying razors by subscription.

evidence_quote: While at the time of the scare the company's market share collapsed from 35 percent to 8 percent, it rebounded in less than a year
prompt: A maker of the best-selling over-the-counter painkiller learns that some bottles in one metropolitan area were poisoned by an unknown person after leaving the factory; the company's own plants appear unaffected. Proposal (1982): withdraw the product from shelves nationwide, halt its production and advertising, and later relaunch it in tamper-resistant packaging. Risks raised: the recall will cost a very large sum for a problem that may be local; the brand may not recover its market share; competitors will take the shelf space; withdrawing the product may signal that it is dangerous.

evidence_quote: The Galaxy Note is a commercial success
prompt: A phone maker sees that its smartphones have screens of about four inches, and considers a phone with a screen of more than five inches that comes with a stylus, sitting between a phone and a tablet. Proposal (2011): announce and sell the large phone as a premium device, alongside its existing line. Risks raised: reviewers may call a screen that size too big for a phone; few buyers may want a stylus; the device may be too small to replace a tablet and too large to replace a phone; it may take sales from the maker's other phones.

evidence_quote: pioneered selling cut-price PCs directly to customers, managing its supply chain and electronic commerce. The company rose rapidly during the 1990s
prompt: A student runs a small business assembling IBM-compatible computers from parts and selling them directly to customers, without stores or resellers, at prices below established brands. Proposal (1984): incorporate the company, keep selling only by direct order, and grow from the revenue. Risks raised: buyers may want to see and try a computer before buying; the established makers have large sales channels and brands; a business with no stores has no service network; supplier parts may be hard to get on credit.

evidence_quote: quickly became the world's best-selling wearable device
prompt: A phone and computer maker has never sold a watch. Smartwatches already exist from other makers and have sold modestly. Proposal (2015): release a watch that works with the maker's phone, in several materials and price levels, with health and fitness tracking and a small app store. Risks raised: earlier smartwatches have sold poorly; the watch needs the phone to be useful; battery life will be about one day; buyers may not see a need for a second screen on the wrist.

evidence_quote: The millionth Fiat 500 was produced in 2012
prompt: A carmaker with weak finances considers a small city car whose styling recalls its own best-loved small car of 1957, built on the platform of an existing small car. Proposal (2007): launch it at a price above the platform-mate, with many trim and personalization options. Risks raised: styling that looks backward may date quickly; buyers may not pay more than for the platform-mate; the company's recent models have sold poorly; small cars carry thin margins.

evidence_quote: The Cayenne had proved commercially successful
prompt: A sports-car maker with a small range and a loyal enthusiast following considers a large luxury crossover SUV, co-developed with a larger group and built on a shared platform. Proposal (2002): launch it as a high-priced model with a powerful engine and off-road ability under the sports-car brand. Risks raised: loyal customers may see an SUV as a betrayal of the brand; the first-year cost is high; a heavy vehicle may damage the sports image; established luxury SUV makers are strong.

evidence_quote: The investment from McDonald's allowed the firm to quickly expand, from 16 restaurants in 1998 to over 500 by 2005.
prompt: A fast-food giant is offered a chance to take a minority stake in a chain of 16 restaurants that sells large burritos made to order, at a higher price than fast food. Proposal (1998): invest, with the right to invest more later, and let the chain run independently. Risks raised: the chain is tiny and may not scale; the food needs more skilled workers and is slower than the giant's own; the price is above the giant's core menu; management attention may be diverted.

evidence_quote: As of 2025, Costco is the third-largest retailer in the world
prompt: A new retailer plans a no-frills warehouse that sells a limited range of goods in bulk at low markup, and charges an annual membership fee to shoppers. It opens its first location in 1983 against a larger competitor already operating that format. Proposal (1983): open more warehouses and sell most goods at a small margin, relying on membership fees for profit. Risks raised: shoppers may not pay a fee to shop; an earlier competitor has more locations and cash; thin margins leave no room for errors; large warehouses need big sites and customers who will buy in bulk.

evidence_quote: This makes the 777 the best-selling wide-body
prompt: An airliner maker with a leading wide-body jet considers an all-new twin-engine aircraft sized between its two existing wide-bodies, designed with eight major airlines in the room from the start. Proposal (1990): launch the program on the strength of an order from one airline for 34 aircraft, at a very large cost. Risks raised: a twin-engine jet on long overwater routes needs aviation authorities' approval that has not been granted; development cost is large; designing with airlines may add changes and delays; a rival is also building new models.

evidence_quote: The Model 3 was the world's best-selling plug-in electric car in 2018.
prompt: An electric-car maker has sold only two expensive vehicles in small numbers and has little experience of mass production. Proposal (2016): unveil a much cheaper electric sedan, take refundable deposits, and begin production the next year at far higher volumes than the company has built. Risks raised: it has never produced at that volume; the battery supply must be scaled up sharply; deposits are refundable and may not become sales; a lower price will leave little margin.

evidence_quote: Demand for PlayStation 4 was strong.
prompt: A console maker's previous generation was late and expensive, and it has lost ground to a rival. Proposal (2013): launch the next console at a price below its rival's, with standard PC-like hardware that is easy for developers to build for, and allow used games and offline play. Risks raised: the rival has a strong head start in online services; a lower price will reduce margin per unit; the maker's own studios have little new software at launch; consumers may be spending less on dedicated consoles.

evidence_quote: Since the release of Ryzen, AMD's CPU market share has increased while Intel's appears to have stagnated or regressed.
prompt: A processor maker that is far smaller than its main rival has fallen behind in desktop performance after a disappointing earlier design. Proposal (2017): launch a new desktop line built on an all-new architecture, with many more cores at lower prices than the rival's equivalents. Risks raised: its last all-new design underperformed; the rival could cut prices or launch faster chips; software may not use extra cores; the company's finances leave no room for a second miss.

evidence_quote: in the device's first year on sale, "millions" of units had sold
prompt: A search company wants to put its video and music services on televisions. Earlier attempts at a television device have sold poorly. Proposal (2013): sell a small, very cheap HDMI dongle that has no remote, and that plays content sent to it from the buyer's phone or computer, with an open kit for other developers. Risks raised: no remote or on-screen menu may confuse buyers; the price leaves almost no margin; few apps support it at launch; established streaming boxes already have large app catalogs.

evidence_quote: In June 2015, Duolingo announced that it had raised $45 million from a Series D funding round led by Google Capital, bringing its total funding to $83.3 million. The round valued the company at around $470 million, with 100 million registered users globally
prompt: A university professor and a student want to teach languages to anyone for free, through a web app with short lessons. They consider a nonprofit but judge it unsustainable. Their early revenue idea is that learners translate real web content as they learn, and the work is sold to publishers. Proposal (2009): build the product, keep learning free for all, and look for revenue later. Risks raised: translations by learners may be poor; free learners may not become paying customers; established paid language courses are much more polished; the revenue model is unproven.

evidence_quote: Samsung suspended sales of the Galaxy Note 7 and announced an informal recall on 2 September 2016, following the discovery of a manufacturing defect in the phones' batteries
prompt: A phone maker's large-screen flagship line sells well. A rival is expected to unveil a new flagship in September. Proposal (2016): release the next large-screen phone in August, earlier than in previous years, with a larger battery in a thin body, a new iris scanner and water resistance, and ship it in volume worldwide. Risks raised: the schedule leaves less time for testing; the battery is larger in a body that is thinner; a new biometric sensor is untested at volume; a defect would be costly at global scale.

evidence_quote: Sales for the Cube were much lower than expected.
prompt: A computer maker that recovered from the brink of collapse has eleven profitable quarters behind it. Proposal (2000): launch a small, silent, fanless desktop in a clear acrylic case, priced above its popular tower, with no expansion slots and few upgrade options. Risks raised: it costs more than a faster tower with expansion slots; the case design is hard to manufacture without flaws; buyers who want to upgrade will not accept the lack of slots; the price is above its popular all-in-one model.

evidence_quote: Sales of the Phaeton fell far short of expectations.
prompt: A mass-market carmaker is the largest in its region and wants to enter the premium class with a very large luxury sedan under its own, mass-market brand name, priced at the level of the established premium rivals. Proposal (2002): build a dedicated factory and launch the sedan worldwide, with a large engine, advanced suspension and top-quality materials. Risks raised: buyers pay for the badge of the premium makers; the brand has no luxury image; the new model is expensive to build at low volume; luxury buyers may not accept a mass-market name.

evidence_quote: The C5 has been described as "one of the great marketing bombs of postwar British industry"
prompt: A British home-computer entrepreneur wants to sell a small, battery-powered, pedal-assisted single-seat tricycle that drivers can use without a licence, priced just below 400 pounds, with several parts sold as optional extras. A large appliance maker has agreed to assemble it. Proposal (1985): unveil it at a launch event in January and sell it by mail order in large numbers. Risks raised: its top speed is only 15 miles per hour; range is short and there is no weather protection; safety groups may object to a vehicle that sits low among traffic; British winters limit use.

evidence_quote: Membership ballooned to over three million subscribers by June 2018, but the service began to suffer from financial issues
prompt: A cinema-subscription service, in which members pay a monthly fee and the company pays theaters the full ticket price for each film seen, has a small number of members at a higher monthly price. A new owner has the cash to subsidize it. Proposal (2017): cut the price to about ten dollars a month for one film a day and grow membership rapidly, then earn from data and from deals with studios and theaters. Risks raised: the company will pay full price for every ticket and the fee does not cover the cost; the new revenue streams are unproven; heavy users will cost more than they pay; theater chains may refuse to cooperate.

evidence_quote: The format's poor reception from consumers resulted in major financial losses for Circuit City
prompt: An electronics retailer with many stores sees the movie rental market and a new high-capacity disc format. Proposal (1998): launch, with partners, a disc format that costs a few dollars to buy and can be watched for 48 hours, after which the customer pays a fee for more viewing time; the discs play only on special players that cost more than standard disc players and that call a phone line. Risks raised: studios and electronics makers must agree to support a new format; the players cost more than the standard players; the discs cannot be played on standard players; customers dislike paying for repeated viewing.

evidence_quote: While popular with college students and young professionals, the company failed soon after the burst of the dot-com bubble
prompt: Two young investment bankers want to deliver videos, games, snacks, books and coffee within an hour in major cities, with free delivery and no minimum order. Proposal (1998): raise venture money, employ delivery staff directly, and expand to more cities quickly. Risks raised: free delivery of small orders costs more than the margin on them; each city needs staff and vehicles; the company must employ many delivery staff directly; customers may use the service only when it is subsidized.

evidence_quote: Windows 8 garnered a mixed to negative reception upon launch.
prompt: The maker of the dominant desktop operating system sees tablets taking market share from PCs. Proposal (2012): replace the traditional desktop start menu with a full-screen, touch-first start screen on all PCs, including those with a keyboard and mouse, and add a tablet app store. Risks raised: corporate and desktop users may find the change confusing and will not want a touch interface on a non-touch PC; the training and support cost for businesses is high; developers must be convinced to write for the new interface; there is no easy way to go back to the old desktop.

evidence_quote: Following public outcry, government investigations and class-action lawsuits in 2005 and 2006, Sony BMG partially addressed the scandal with consumer settlements, a recall of about 10% of the affected CDs
prompt: A major record company is losing sales to copying of audio discs on computers. Proposal (2005): ship millions of new audio discs with copy-protection software that installs itself on the buyer's computer when the disc is played, to limit copying and ripping. Risks raised: software that installs without clear consent may be seen as intrusive; the software may be hard to remove; security researchers could find weaknesses; customers may object to being treated as thieves.

evidence_quote: Apple Maps received considerable criticism after its launch on September 19, 2012, due to wrong and inaccurate information
prompt: A phone maker relies on a rival's mapping application on its phones and wants more control. Proposal (2012): replace the rival's maps with its own mapping app as the default on all new and updated phones in the fall, with turn-by-turn navigation, 3D views and voice assistant support, built from several data providers. Risks raised: the new maps have a lot less data than the established app; place and business information may be wrong in places; users may be annoyed when their working app is removed; a rival product will no longer be available by default.

evidence_quote: Intel offered to replace processors to users who could prove that they were affected.
prompt: A chip maker finds that its new processor returns slightly wrong answers for some rare floating-point divisions. Its own analysis says a typical user would meet the error about once in many thousands of years. Proposal (1994): state that the flaw is not serious, and offer replacement chips only to users who can show that their work is affected, rather than to everyone who asks. Risks raised: users cannot easily show that they are affected; the problem is being widely discussed; a replacement for every chip would cost a very large sum; the company's reputation may suffer if buyers believe it is hiding a defect.

evidence_quote: Sony initially resisted licensing Beta, limiting its market reach.
prompt: An electronics maker has launched a home video cassette recorder with a smaller tape, better picture quality and a one-hour tape, and a rival maker is preparing a competing format with longer tapes. Proposal (1975): keep the format proprietary, license it only to a few partners, and rely on its picture quality and an early lead. Risks raised: the rival is licensing its format to many makers, which will spread players and lower prices; one-hour tapes will not record a full film or sports event; a format with fewer manufacturers may have fewer pre-recorded titles; the rival's format may become the standard.

evidence_quote: Only 140,000 units were sold during the lifetime of the product, and in the later years the Segway PT only made up 1.5% of total company profit.
prompt: An inventor has built a two-wheeled, self-balancing electric transporter that the rider steers by leaning, meant to replace short car trips and walking in cities. Proposal (2001): launch it to consumers at about 5,000 dollars and sell it widely in cities. Risks raised: the price is well above a bicycle, a scooter or a used car; riders need time to learn to balance on it; rules for sidewalks and roads may not allow it; it does not carry cargo or a second person.

evidence_quote: After many missed deadlines and questionable results from a trial clinic at Safeway's corporate offices, the deal was terminated in 2015.
prompt: A large supermarket chain is approached by a young health-technology company whose founder says its device can run many blood tests from a few drops of blood, quickly and cheaply. Proposal (2012): invest about 350 million dollars to fit clinics into hundreds of its stores that would offer the tests, in return for exclusivity. Risks raised: the technology has not been shown in published studies; the chain has no medical expertise; the company will not share its methods; regulators may later question the tests.

evidence_quote: In June 2011, Specific Media Group and Justin Timberlake jointly purchased the company for approximately $35 million.
prompt: A media company is offered a fast-growing social-networking website that started two years earlier and has a large young audience. Proposal (2005): buy it for 580 million dollars, to combine its audience with the company's advertising and media business. Risks raised: the price is high for a site that young; tastes in social sites can change quickly; other social sites compete for the same users; turning rapid audience growth into advertising revenue is unproven.
